Did Luke Rewrite History? The Historical Problems of Luke–Acts:  The author of Luke opens his Gospel by declaring that he investigated earlier traditions to produce an orderly account of Jesus' life (Luke 1:1–4). Yet historical-critical scholarship has identified several instances where his narrative diverges from earlier Gospel traditions and external historical records.  Most scholars date Luke–Acts to approximately 80–100 AD, although later dates have also been proposed. Its author relied extensively upon Mark, incorporated additional traditions, and constructed a continuous history extending from Jesus' birth to the expansion of Christianity throughout the Roman Empire.  The first problem is Luke's reconstruction of Jesus' ministry. In Mark 6:1–6, Jesus returns to Nazareth after an established period of preaching and healing throughout Galilee. His hometown rejects him, but the incident ends without an attempted execution.  Luke 4:16–30 relocates this encounter to the beginning of Jesus' public ministry and dramatically expands it. Jesus reads from Isaiah, announces the fulfillment of scripture, and provokes an angry crowd that attempts to throw him from a cliff.  The editorial alteration is especially revealing because Luke 4:23 refers to miracles already performed in Capernaum, even though Luke has not yet narrated Jesus' ministry there.  Matthew R. Crawford, in Connecting Gospels (2018), examines this rewriting and demonstrates how Luke relocated the earlier Markan narrative while introducing the attempted execution. Joel B. Green, in The Theology of the Gospel of Luke, explains that the Nazareth episode serves as a programmatic introduction to Jesus' entire mission.  Luke's narrative arrangement reflects his theological interpretation of Jesus' ministry rather than a straightforward reproduction of Mark's chronology.  The resurrection narratives present another problem. In Mark 16:7, the women are instructed that Jesus will meet his disciples in Galilee. Matthew 28:16–20 develops this tradition by describing the disciples traveling to a mountain in Galilee, where the resurrected Jesus appears to them.  However, Luke 24 places the resurrection appearances in and around Jerusalem. His Jesus appears to disciples traveling toward Emmaus, subsequently reveals himself to the assembled disciples in Jerusalem, and instructs them to remain in the city until they receive heavenly power.  This geographical difference is significant because Jerusalem functions as the theological center of Luke–Acts. Jesus' ministry progresses toward Jerusalem, and the Christian mission subsequently expands from Jerusalem toward Rome.  Luke also provides the only canonical Gospel account explicitly narrating Jesus' ascension. In Luke 24, the sequence appears to place the ascension on resurrection day, while Acts 1 introduces forty days of resurrection appearances before narrating Jesus' departure.  Henk Jan de Jonge, writing in New Testament Studies (2013), challenges the usual interpretation of this chronological difference. He argues that both accounts can place the ascension on resurrection day, with the forty days referring to subsequent appearances. The very existence of this debate illustrates the importance of examining Luke's narrative construction rather than assuming that the two accounts supply a transparent chronology.  The problems continue into Acts, where Luke's account can be compared with independently surviving historical records.  Acts 5:36–37 attributes a speech to Gamaliel in which he mentions a rebel named Theudas, followed by Judas the Galilean, who arose during the census.  Yet the historian Josephus, in Jewish Antiquities 20.97–99, places Theudas's revolt during the governorship of Cuspius Fadus, approximately 44–46 AD. Judas the Galilean's uprising occurred during the census of 6 AD.  Luke reverses their historical sequence and places a reference to Theudas within a speech set before the period in which Josephus records his revolt.  Some scholars propose that Acts refers to another otherwise unattested rebel also named Theudas. The discrepancy remains one of the most significant chronological problems in Acts.  A further difficulty appears in Luke's birth narrative, which associates Jesus' birth with Quirinius's census in 6 AD. Matthew instead places the birth during the reign of Herod the Great, who died in 4 BC. These dates are separated by approximately a decade, and no independently attested earlier census of Quirinius resolves the discrepancy.  Richard Pervo, in Acts: A Commentary (2009), argues that Acts should be read as a sophisticated literary account shaped by its author's theological interests rather than treated as an independently reliable chronological record. His broader reconstruction also considers whether the author used Josephus and other written sources.  –––  The conservative historical-critical response:  Craig S. Keener, in Acts: An Exegetical Commentary (2012–2015), and Darrell L. Bock, in his commentary on Luke, argue that Luke's literary rearrangements must be understood according to ancient historiographical conventions. Ancient historians regularly reorganized their sources, condensed events, and reconstructed speeches without necessarily intending to falsify history. The question is whether Luke preserves authentic historical traditions beneath his theological presentation.  Regarding Jesus' rejection at Nazareth, Bock acknowledges that Luke deliberately relocated the episode from its position in Mark 6 to the beginning of Jesus' ministry. However, he argues that Luke's promise to provide an "orderly account" does not necessarily mean strict chronological sequence. The Nazareth episode introduces the themes that dominate Luke's Gospel: Jesus' prophetic mission, rejection by his own people, and the extension of God's salvation beyond Israel. On this interpretation, Luke rearranged a genuine historical incident to establish the theological framework of his narrative. The relocation is demonstrable, but it does not establish that the underlying event was invented. The attempted execution remains a separate question because it lacks independent attestation.  Regarding the resurrection appearances, conservative scholars argue that Matthew's Galilean appearances and Luke's Jerusalem appearances need not be mutually exclusive. Acts 1:3 describes Jesus appearing over forty days, allowing sufficient time for appearances in both locations. Luke concentrates on Jerusalem because it becomes the geographical starting point of the Christian mission in Acts, while Matthew emphasizes Galilee because of its association with Jesus' ministry and the commissioning of his disciples. Luke's command to remain in Jerusalem can be understood as a final instruction before Pentecost, following any earlier journey to Galilee.  The apparent contradiction between Luke 24 and Acts 1 concerning the ascension is addressed similarly. Bock and other conservative interpreters understand Luke 24 as compressing the post-resurrection period, whereas Acts explicitly supplies its forty-day duration. Since Luke does not explicitly state that every event in the chapter occurred on resurrection Sunday, the absence of a chronological transition does not necessarily establish that the author intended two incompatible dates.  Regarding the census of Quirinius, the conservative response is more complicated. Quirinius's documented census occurred in 6 AD, approximately a decade after Herod's death. Wayne Brindle, in The Census and Quirinius: Luke 2:2 (1984), argues that the Greek word prōtē may permit the passage to refer to a census preceding Quirinius's famous registration. Other scholars have proposed an earlier, otherwise unattested census or administrative involvement by Quirinius before 6 AD.  David J. Armitage, in Detaching the Census (2018), offers another approach, suggesting that Luke 2:1–5 could function as a chronological digression describing a later registration rather than dating Jesus' birth itself.  These proposals attempt to reconcile Luke with established Roman chronology, but none has achieved general scholarly acceptance. An earlier census matching Luke's description remains unverified, and the proposed grammatical interpretations are disputed. Even conservative commentators such as Bock acknowledge that no definitive resolution has been established.  Regarding Theudas, Keener examines the possibility that Gamaliel referred to another revolutionary bearing the same name, or that Josephus preserved an inaccurate chronology (Josephus isn't always correct). Judea experienced numerous disturbances, and the surviving historical record is incomplete.  However, Keener ultimately considers the proposed second Theudas unpersuasive and accepts that Luke probably confused the chronology. His argument is that an identifiable chronological error does not invalidate an entire historical work, especially when its author demonstrates accurate knowledge elsewhere.  Colin J. Hemer, in The Book of Acts in the Setting of Hellenistic History (1989), develops this broader defense through extensive comparison with archaeology, inscriptions, Roman administration, and Mediterranean geography. Acts correctly employs specialized titles such as politarchs for Thessalonian magistrates and Asiarchs for provincial officials. The Gallio inscription independently confirms the proconsul named in Acts 18 and provides a chronological anchor around 51–52 AD.  Hemer argues that these correspondences demonstrate substantial familiarity with the first-century Roman world and support the possibility that Luke drew upon reliable historical information, including eyewitness traditions.  The conservative historical-critical position is that Luke's narrative contains genuine historical material presented through the literary and theological conventions of ancient historiography. His chronological rearrangements are not automatically fabrications, geographical differences can sometimes be reconciled, and occasional errors do not establish general unreliability.  The strongest limitation to this defense is that demonstrating historical competence cannot independently establish the accuracy of every narrated event. Even if Luke knew Roman geography and administration remarkably well, the historicity of particular speeches, miracles, and uniquely Lukan episodes must still be evaluated on their own evidence.

The agency, chaired by Martin Koyabe, is intended to strengthen national cyber-threat coordination and the capacity of the National Cybersecurity Operations Centre.  The government is adding the agency to an existing cybersecurity framework that includes the Communications Authority's National Kenya Computer Incident Response Team Coordination Centre and the National Computer and Cybercrimes Coordination Committee. The board's immediate assignment includes developing human-resource instruments and establishing management structures ahead of January 2027.

Circle K cuts DevOps incident triage time by up to 75% with Amazon Bedrock  Circle K operates more than 17,200 convenience and fuel retail stores in 27 countries. Its DevOps team monitors infrastructure across multiple AWS accounts with Grafana. Prior to automation, a typical incident triage required 45–60 minutes of manual investigation. The manual process involved pulling logs, checking service health, and correlating symptoms across several tools. That investigation burden sits within a retail operation spread across 27 countries, while the monitoring team works across multiple AWS accounts; the scale and distributed setup help explain why a repeatable triage process matters. The old 45–60-minute window was not just a quick alert check: it included gathering logs, checking service health and comparing symptoms across tools. Because the incidents concern infrastructure monitored by the DevOps team, the time spent piecing together those signals directly affects the engineers responsible for understanding each alert.  Common alerts include container restarts, elevated error rates, latency spikes and failed deployments. When Grafana publishes an alert to Amazon SNS, the message is forwarded to an SQS queue, triggering the new workflow. A Lambda process checks the SQS queue, takes the alert information from its message, and starts an Amazon Bedrock Flow. The alert types range from container restarts and failed deployments to elevated errors and latency spikes, so the workflow is designed to begin from several kinds of operational symptoms. SNS and SQS form the handoff between the Grafana alert and the process that investigates it; the alert is therefore routed into the workflow rather than requiring the described investigation to begin by manually gathering information. Once the queued alert is handled, Lambda extracts its payload and invokes the Flow, connecting the monitoring signal to the automated investigation.  The automated triage system is built on Amazon Bedrock, a fully managed foundation‑model service. It uses an agentic AI architecture that investigates each incident autonomously and posts a structured summary to Slack. Three parallel agents gather data: the AWSResourceExplorerAgent checks ECS task status, ALB target health and CloudWatch metrics and logs. The OpenSearchExplorerAgent accesses a knowledge base of product cards describing each service and its dependencies. A GitHubExplorerAgent then searches the affected service’s repositories for code, infrastructure definitions and recent commits. These sources cover different parts of an incident: infrastructure status and monitoring information come from AWSResourceExplorerAgent, while the knowledge base supplies service and dependency descriptions. The repository search adds code, infrastructure definitions and recent commits for the affected service, bringing a further kind of context into the investigation. The agents work in parallel before the GitHub search takes place, so the workflow draws on both infrastructure and service knowledge before looking through the affected service’s repositories. Bedrock provides the managed foundation-model service beneath this architecture, while the agents carry out the separate information-gathering tasks.  Outputs from the three agents are merged in an AnalysisPrompt node that makes a single model call without attached tools. The combined result is posted to Slack, giving engineers a concise, actionable summary. The AnalysisPrompt step brings the agents’ findings together in one model call, rather than attaching tools to that final call. That combined output gives the investigation a single summary destination in Slack, where engineers can review the structured result of the autonomous triage. The division between gathering information and combining outputs is explicit: agents perform the searches and checks, and the AnalysisPrompt node consolidates what they return. For engineers receiving an alert, this means the described workflow delivers a structured summary after collecting infrastructure, service-dependency and repository context.  The new workflow delivers a 67–75 percent improvement over prior triage times. The reported improvement compares the new triage workflow with the earlier 45–60-minute manual investigation period. The percentage improvement compares the new workflow with the previous manual triage process, rather than with a different kind of operational task. The earlier process took 45–60 minutes, so a 67–75 percent improvement represents a substantial reduction in the investigation time engineers spent on a typical incident. The reported 67–75 percent improvement illustrates the difference from the former 45–60-minute investigation window. These figures describe triage and investigation time; they indicate a faster path to an incident summary, not a separate measured figure for how long every incident takes to resolve.  Circle K selected Bedrock because it aligned with existing IAM policies, VPC configurations and logging pipelines. The team had evaluated open‑source agent frameworks but rejected them due to the overhead of model hosting, prompt versioning, tool orchestration and security controls. The fit with existing IAM, VPC and logging arrangements was a reason for choosing Bedrock, linking the selection to systems and controls Circle K already had in place. The alternative frameworks were not rejected because they lacked a named capability in these facts; the stated concern was the work involved in hosting models, managing prompts and orchestration, and maintaining security controls. That comparison shows the decision involved operational overhead as well as the availability of an agent framework: Circle K weighed the extra responsibilities against Bedrock’s fit with existing configurations. The existing-policy fit is relevant to the team responsible for operating the workflow, while the listed overheads describe the tasks it wanted to avoid taking on with an open-source framework.  Amazon Bedrock does not share customer data with model providers nor use it to train foundation models, addressing data‑privacy concerns. This data-handling policy is directly relevant to a system that investigates incidents using operational information and then produces summaries for engineers. The stated protection has two parts: customer data is not shared with model providers, and it is not used to train foundation models. Those assurances address one consideration for teams adopting a foundation-model service, although the facts also describe Circle K’s separate reliance on existing IAM, VPC and logging configurations.  The automated system processes alerts from Grafana, enriches them with infrastructure and code context, and delivers a concise report to engineers, streamlining the incident response cycle. By reducing investigation time, Circle K can resolve incidents faster, minimizing service disruption across its global store network. The workflow connects the monitoring setup across AWS accounts to a sequence that routes alerts, gathers infrastructure and repository information, combines the findings and sends a summary to Slack. Its intended users include the DevOps engineers who monitor the infrastructure and receive the structured Slack summary after an incident is investigated. The time improvement matters against the prior manual baseline of 45–60 minutes, while the reported percentage reduction describes the change in triage time rather than a separate measure of store performance. Circle K’s footprint spans more than 17,200 convenience and fuel retail stores in 27 countries, giving the monitoring and triage system a broad operational context.  The adoption of Bedrock demonstrates how managed AI services can be integrated into existing cloud operations without extensive new security engineering. In this case, the documented basis for integration is Bedrock’s fit with Circle K’s existing IAM policies, VPC configurations and logging pipelines. That fit contrasts with the overheads the team associated with open-source frameworks, including security controls as well as model hosting, prompt versioning and tool orchestration. The example therefore centers on choosing a managed service that works with established cloud arrangements, rather than building and operating every part of the agent infrastructure independently. The described approach combines Bedrock, a fully managed foundation-model service, with agents that check infrastructure, consult service knowledge and search repositories. For Circle K’s DevOps team, the result is an automated investigation workflow that starts from Grafana alerts and returns a structured summary, with the reported triage-time improvement measured against the prior manual process.

sample_tweets.text: Italy Alert 🇮🇹  NoName057(16) SCADA Attack Alert: Borsoi Filling Line 2026

The post is accurate on the core facts, but the framing deserves some unpacking. This is the second wave in under a month. In mid-October, hackers hit roughly seven hundred supermarkets across France — Carrefour, Intermarché, Monoprix, Coopérative U — raising temps to fifty degrees Celsius, causing fires and tens of millions of euros in losses. Today's wave is smaller per country but wider geographically: over a hundred stores across Belgium, Luxembourg, Sweden, Ireland, Estonia, the Netherlands, and Finland. Delhaize lost about forty stores, Carrefour fifteen, SuperValu thirteen in Ireland, Coop seven in Sweden. One Delhaize store in Hoeilaart put its loss at a hundred thousand euros.  The mechanism is the same in both waves. Commercial refrigeration runs on supervisory controllers — Danfoss AK-SM and AK-SC, Copeland and Dixell XWEB — whose web management interfaces were left directly reachable from the public internet so technicians could adjust temperatures remotely. Attackers didn't need malware. They just logged in with weak or bypassed credentials and flipped units into continuous defrost mode. Claroty's Team82 published research on exactly these Danfoss flaws in August — a hidden "code-of-the-day" authentication bypass rated eight point two, plus command injection — and Danfoss shipped firmware R4.3.1 to fix them. But Forescout's October scan still found nearly thirteen thousand exposed refrigeration services across six thousand public IPs in ninety-nine countries, and eighty percent of the Danfoss StoreView instances were running firmware older than the patched version. The Danfoss AK-SM 800 has been end-of-life since May 2021 with no patch path at all.  On the US military angle — that's real too, but softer. Reuters reported October twenty-ninth that the Pentagon is treating late-August freezer malfunctions at about six commissaries — Fort Huachuca, Fort Irwin, Travis, F.E. Warren, Naval Station Newport, Columbus — as a suspected cyberattack, with temperatures cranked overnight. Two unnamed officials told Nextgov they suspect Iran-linked hackers, and Cyber Command is coordinating with French law enforcement. But the Pentagon hasn't publicly confirmed attribution or even that hacking caused it. So that part of the post is reporting on a suspicion, not an established fact.  Who's behind the European attacks? Nobody knows. No group has claimed credit, no ransom demand surfaced, and Reuters couldn't establish any link between today's wave and October's. SentinelOne's Tom Hegel calls it a working theory that it looks like sabotage rather than extortion — cheap, deniable disruption with no financial ask. Russia is the obvious hypothesis given its sabotage record in Europe, but that's inference, not evidence. Separately, pro-Russian hacktivist groups Z-Pentest Alliance and NoName057(16) had already claimed over twenty refrigeration attacks this year before the French incident — fruit storage, wineries, food processors in Spain and Italy — using the identical method of changing temperature and defrost settings through exposed interfaces.  Is this a huge coordinated campaign or a couple of stories blown up? It's neither extreme. It's a known, widespread vulnerability class being exploited at scale — the second confirmed wave of it. The underlying exposure is genuinely massive and global, not European. But the attacks themselves are opportunistic exploitation of end-of-life hardware that should have been taken offline, not a sophisticated novel intrusion. The BBC also explicitly noted there's no evidence domestic smart fridges are being targeted — this is commercial and industrial operational technology, not your kitchen.  One thing worth sitting with: the EU's food commissioner called it a deliberate attempt to disrupt the food supply chain. If that read is right, the chilling implication isn't the spoiled meat — it's that the same controllers run hospitals, pharma cold chains, and data centers.

I've been researching the recent attacks on commercial refrigeration systems. In October there was a French wave that hit hundreds of stores. A subsequent wave hit stores in Belgium, Luxembourg, Sweden, Ireland, the Netherlands, Estonia, and Finland.   Attribution remains open. No ransom demands, no data theft, no claims. The attacks left almost no distinctive technical fingerprints beyond the exploitation of widely known, internet-exposed legacy controllers.  If I had to guess? Pro-Russian hacktivist groups (primarily Z-Pentest Alliance and/or NoName057(16))  The incidents illustrate a classic OT problem: internet exposure of legacy controllers with weak security created an easily exploitable surface for disruptive attacks. The fix is easy but very inconvenient.

러시아 연계 해커들, 공장에 불이 나고 수도관이 터지게 만들었다.  그런데 공격에 사용된 방법은 생각보다 복잡하지 않았습니다.  블룸버그가 2026년 10월 27일 보도한 조사에 따르면, 친러시아 해커 그룹들이 서방 여러 나라의 수도시설, 공장, 식품 생산시설을 공격해 실제 운영 차질과 물리적 피해를 일으켰습니다.  대표적인 사례가 덴마크 투레뷔입니다.  2024년 12월, 수도시설의 제어시스템 설정이 바뀌면서 450가구의 물 공급이 중단됐습니다. 다음 날에는 수압이 급격히 올라가 지하 배관까지 파열됐습니다.  당시 시스템의 비밀번호는 '1234'였습니다.  미국 로스앤젤레스 인근 육가공시설에서도 냉동설비가 중단돼 약 900kg의 육류가 상했고, 암모니아 누출로 작업자들이 대피했습니다. 스페인에서는 화장장 설비 중단과 변압기 제조시설 화재도 발생했습니다.  이 공격에서 주목할 점은 해커들이 반드시 고도의 기술을 사용한 것은 아니라는 사실입니다.  미국 FBI·CISA와 국제 보안기관의 2025년 12월 공동 보고서에 따르면, 이들은 인터넷에 노출된 원격접속 장치(VNC)를 찾고, 기본 비밀번호나 약한 비밀번호를 이용해 산업시설의 제어 화면(HMI)에 접근했습니다.  VNC는 다른 컴퓨터의 화면을 원격으로 보고 조작하는 프로그램입니다. HMI는 작업자가 공장 기계나 수도 펌프의 상태를 확인하고 조작하는 화면입니다.  CARR, NoName057(16), Z-Pentest, Sector16 등은 서로 공격을 주장하거나 방법을 공유하는 관계로 확인됐습니다. 다만 모든 공격이 러시아 정부의 직접 지시로 이뤄졌다고 단정할 수는 없습니다.  여기서 더 중요한 문제는 공격자의 기술 수준보다 산업시설의 기본 보안입니다.  정부 기관들도 공격이 상대적으로 단순하고 평균적인 피해 규모는 낮다고 평가하면서, 취약한 시설에서는 실제 물리적 피해가 발생할 수 있다고 경고했습니다.  제 생각에는 산업시설의 보안은 외부 침입을 막는 것만으로 충분하지 않습니다. 원격접속을 제한하고, 비정상적인 제어 명령을 감시하며, 시스템이 공격받아도 현장에서 안전하게 운영을 이어갈 수 있어야 합니다.  여러분은 산업시설 보안에서 가장 먼저 바꿔야 할 것이 기본적인 접속 관리일까요, 아니면 공격을 받아도 설비가 멈추지 않는 복구 체계일까요?  #사이버보안 #산업보안 #핵심기반시설

When hackers break into networks, it's achieved by using software vulnerabilities less than 30% of the time. That's not just zero-day exploits, that counting any vulnerabilities at all. My moderately informed midwit take is that I think the reason 'cyber letters of marque' constantly keeps getting re-floated is because the US government has a problem it has neither the time, money, headcount, nor risk appetite to address.  You have a bunch of hostile foreign threat actors hacking into US infrastructure, but not in a way which constitutes an "attack" and that the US would be comfortable responding to with much more than what they're already doing. It's mostly just nuisance stuff like cybercrime & espionage, rather than "attacks" in the military or terrorist sense.  One huge issues right now is that North Korea have basically decided that cybercrime is central to their economic policy, so are encouraging people to join the military and commit crimes for a living.   DPRK's cyber capacity is growing at an unprecedented rate, and the headcount of their cyber force is absolutely huge. Currently they're mostly concerned with stealing cryptocurrency, which isn't not even remotely important to the US economy. But that doesn't mean that DPRK can't quickly re-task their capacity towards something more damaging.  Typically, the solution to unreachable cyber actors who become too problematic is for the state to hack them, take all their money, flatten their infrastructure, and then public indict them.  You can't really do that as easily with state-sponsored actors, because launching destructive cyber attacks against a hostile foreign military could be considered an escalation, regardless of what they did to deserve it (unless they did something that met the bar for an "attack" first).  The US government likely doesn't have that kind of risk appetite. If you start wiping out DPRK military systems, they will consider that an escalation, as will their allies, some of whom have some extremely advanced cyber capabilities and an lot of personnel.  The US military's core cyber capacity is not huge, and its extremely fragmented. You have US Cyber Command, which is a decent size, but not huge. Then a bunch of random military units and contractors all over the place.  Already the US is struggling to deal with DPRK crypto theft and remote workers, Iran attacking critical infrastructure, China embedding themselves in everything they can find. The last thing they need is escalation.  I don't think anyone is vying to be the one to pull the trigger on launching into a direct confrontation with with several extremely powerful cyber actors. I know people love to do the whole "US #1. Most powerful military on the planet" thing. But that hasn't been working out so great for them.  So cyber letters of marque are useful because it allows the US to basically encourage civilians to attack targets for them, increasing US capacity, and also shifting some of the risk off of government and onto civilians.  It's easy to find like 50,000 Jason Borne wannabe goober ass mf'ers who are happy to throw hands at well-resources foreign cybercrime actors, and even hostile state military and intelligence agencies. It might actually even keep the adversaries busy.  It's certainly an idea for the US government, but will likely be a terrible one for just about everyone else, including the US public. It's essentially just a way of turning random pentesters into state-certified cannon fodder, and everyone else just gets caught in the crossfire.  I don't know exactly what would happen if something like that actually gets approved and operationalized, but I just know it's going to be absolutely hilarious in the worst way possible.  Just imagine a bunch of Nessus monkeys at some random pentest mill going toe-to-toe with the MSS, FSB, SVR, or RIGB. The amount of popcorn I'd need for this would exceed the total global corn supply.

"There's interest in bringing back 'letters of marque and reprisal' to counteract the cybercrime that North Korea is committing."  North Korean cyber actors are military and intelligence personnel. If you're gonna go getting yourself into a direct confrontation with a hostile state's military apparatus, I'd say: gl, hf, and make sure you have a decent life insurance policy

I'm relatively confident in predicting that currently, more major breaches are likely to be the result of AI use by the target, not the attacker.  Ransomware actors have been consistently winning for over a decade. They've had so much time to perfect their tradecraft, and non-AI ransomware actors can now blast through entire networks in minutes.  It is extremely unlikely that organizational security has, in 4 years, after decades of failure, matured enough that hackers now somehow need AI to win.  What has likely happened, though, is that organizations have spent the last 4 years falling over themselves to shove AI into everything, negating longstanding security fundamentals.   "only give a user/system the minimum possible access needed to do its job" has become "just give the AI access to everything and give everyone access to the AI".  "use processes with well-defined and easily auditable input and output" has become "the AI correctly processes requests all the time, 60 percent of the time"  "reduce attack surfaces" is now "every department should be vibe coding. It doesn't matter if you've never coded before and don't understand information security. Just make public-facing dashboards, it'll be fine."  I'd say if anything, hackers aren't getting measurably more sophisticated, but the average organization's security posture has gotten exponentially worse.

🚨 Google dismantles XCPE botnet hidden in more than 1.3 million Android TV boxes Google says manufacturer Videostrong Technology intentionally embedded the backdoor into device firmware before the products were sold, giving operators remote access to boxes across more than 200 countries. ⠀ The infected devices were used for: • Residential proxy networks • Advertising fraud • Data theft • Additional malware delivery • Routing criminal traffic through home connections Google seized command-and-control infrastructure, disrupted affiliate malware linked to at least 10 million additional devices and permanently banned Videostrong and its affiliates from producing certified Android devices. Source: https:// cloud.google.com/blog/topics/t hreat-intelligence/shutting-the-door-on-the-xcpe-botnet

🚨🇪🇺 Second wave of cyberattacks manipulates supermarket freezers across Europe Refrigeration systems at stores in Sweden, Belgium, Ireland, Estonia, the Netherlands and Luxembourg were remotely altered, with some units reportedly set to 50°C and switched into defrost mode. ⠀ More than 50 stores were identified in Belgium, while 13 SuperValu locations in Ireland and at least 17 businesses in the Netherlands were affected. Stores removed or discarded chilled and frozen products. ⠀ The attacks follow a similar incident that disrupted refrigeration at around 700 locations in France during October. No group has claimed responsibility, and authorities have not confirmed whether the two campaigns are connected. Source: https:// therecord.media/cyberattack-gr ocery-freezers-europe

🚨 Critical Linux kernel flaw could allow remote root code execution; CVE-2026-98432 A use-after-free vulnerability in the Linux IPv4 TCP handshake path allows an unauthenticated attacker to trigger memory corruption by sending specially timed packets to a listening service. Successful exploitation could crash the system or potentially execute arbitrary code as root. ⠀ • CVSS: 9.8 • Affected: Linux kernel 4.4 and later • Attack vector: Network • Privileges required: None • User interaction: None • Active exploitation: Not reported ⠀ Fixed kernel branches: • 5.10.272 • 5.15.223 • 6.1.190 • 6.6.159 • 6.12.113 • 6.18.56 • 7.2.10 • 7.3 ⠀ Administrators should install their distribution’s updated kernel and reboot to activate the fix. Advisory: https:// access.redhat.com/security/vul nerabilities/RHSB-2026-016

🚨 Synology warns of ongoing C3RB3R ransomware attacks targeting outdated NAS devices Attackers are exploiting a vulnerability patched in December 2024 to breach Synology devices running outdated DiskStation Manager versions, encrypt files and demand ransom payments. ⠀ Victims report files receiving the .L0CK3D extension alongside a read-me3.txt ransom note directing them to purchase a C3RB3R decryptor. ⠀ Synology has not identified the specific vulnerability being exploited. The linked advisory covers: • CVE-2024-10441: Remote code execution • CVE-2024-50629: Arbitrary file read • CVE-2024-10445: Arbitrary file write ⠀ Users should immediately update DSM, enable automatic updates and remove the management interface from direct internet exposure. Source: https://www. bleepingcomputer.com/news/secu rity/synology-warns-customers-of-ongoing-c3rb3r-ransomware-attacks/

🚨🇺🇸 Actor Offering Cryptocurrency Payments for Anthropic and AWS Bedrock API Keys An actor using the handle "daybreak1" is attempting to purchase Anthropic Claude and AWS Bedrock API keys, offering cryptocurrency payments equal to 50% of the usage generated through each key. The actor advertises the following arrangement: • $1,000 in API usage = $500 payment • $2,000 in API usage = $1,000 payment • Cryptocurrency payments • Anthropic and AWS Bedrock keys accepted A screenshot accompanying the listing shows an API management dashboard displaying over $36,000 in available balance. The offer raises concerns about the potential monetization of compromised API credentials and unauthorized AI service consumption. Claim is currently unverified.

🚨🇲🇽 Mexican Government Employee Data Allegedly Leaked, Over 270,000 Records Exposed An actor known as "zerttack" claims to have compromised DeclaraSon, the Government of Sonora's financial and interest disclosure platform used by public officials in Mexico. The actor has published a CSV dataset allegedly containing 270,382 records, including: • Full names and CURP identification numbers • Government departments and employment dependencies • Financial declaration types and version histories • Declaration submission dates and timestamps The records could expose sensitive information about government employees and their official financial disclosures. Claim is currently unverified.

I don’t think it’s accurate
I wasn't trying to, in fairness - I was trying to align it with the original discussion.  It's great we agree on that.
Thank for the random insults, I will enjoy my apparent reputation.
A 2017 classic.  My favourite were the images they produced of Anonymous bombing offices, and then their CMO getting into an argument on Wikipedia when their GenV page got flagged for delegation.

I don't think they're necessarily uninformed. If they don't know details people are doing their job well in cybersecurity.

One of the problems the industry has is decades of crying wolf about everything, cyber pearl habour etc.  The result is most people don't care.  And that's okay.

I did ICS sec for a good while and all the time we'd get Siemens etc saying 'turn off AV, firewalls etc' otherwise they wouldn't do the install.  When pushed back, they'd come back with 'it's fine, we run nuclear power plants like this'.  

It's like, my guys, that is not as reassuring as you think.
Yeah, I don't think they should be concerned about ARTEX and the like.  Ransomware wrecking hospitals for the past decade, sure.
i love the holiday season.  and greggs.
Oh indeed.  But I was talking about the context of people outside the practitioner level.

There's significant issues with cyber vendors sparking panic downstream regarding GenAI, FWIW, in my experience.

Yes there are more vulns and more patching, and yes ShinyHunters are still dicks.
I think this is the best coverage of the PHP thing I've seen still.

In many cases it's not the supermarkets themselves doing this, it's their suppliers - they're banging them in with 4G adapters internet facing to manage them remotely.  Which, as it turns out, isn't a good idea.
Beeb piece: www.bbc.co.uk/news/article...
Threadorama: cyberplace.social/@GossiTheDog...
If anybody wondering - internet facing management interfaces again, unpatched devices too.
I'll admend them - I'm busy.  The vendor hype doesn't match what is being seen across the trenches in my experience, and with cyber insurance provider incident data.

I'm not a victim, just responding to "despite your habit of pretending so".

I wasn't dismissing your experience, FWIW.  I'm sure external IR is busy.  I'm just offering a wider context view where I don't think there's reasons for folks outside to be concerned.

Yep. Each time somebody rolls up with zero trust, XDR, SOAR etc etc and loads of orgs invest heavily, don’t complete the implementation project, and then move on to the next vendor driven fad. 

Don’t get me wrong - raw automation, great, do it. You should have done it fifteen years ago.

I don't think so, largely.  It's the 'you must buy our AI to fight AI' stuff that orgs are spinning their wheels with again, after you must have zero trust, a SOAR, XDR etc.

It may help if orgs weren't neglient with cybersecurity, eg started patching, segmenting networks etc.
